claims.text: A predominantly single-phase, disordered lightweight HEA can combine low density with a high strength-to-weight ratio.
A predominantly single-phase, disordered lightweight HEA can exhibit high corrosion resistance.
A predominantly solid-solution lightweight HEA can exhibit useful mechanical properties and oxidation resistance.
Lattice distortions in the disordered solid solution hinder dislocation motion and thereby strengthen the alloy.
Lattice distortions promote or stabilize a dense, uniform, passivating oxide layer.
The distortion-stabilized oxide layer improves resistance to corrosive attack.
The distortion-stabilized oxide layer improves high-temperature oxidation resistance.
Increasing copper content can promote copper segregation in a lightweight HEA.
Controlled copper addition can induce secondary-phase precipitation.
Segregation or secondary-phase formation reduces or eliminates beneficial lattice distortions.
Segregation or secondary-phase formation deteriorates mechanical performance.
Copper segregation accelerates local corrosion and decreases corrosion resistance as copper content increases.
Segregation or secondary-phase formation deteriorates high-temperature oxidation resistance.
The optimized single-phase alloy should have a higher strength-to-weight ratio than the segregated comparison alloy.
The optimized low-segregation alloy should have a lower self-corrosion current density than the higher-copper segregated alloy.
The optimized single-phase alloy should have better oxidation resistance than the segregated comparison alloy.
The proposed property synergy should cease when segregation or intermetallic phases become predominant.
Alternative strengthening mechanisms, including strengthening from complex precipitates, can dominate independently of a single disordered phase.
